title: When the Winter Turns
premise: Sebastian Nakamura, a late-night radio host grieving their partner Marisol's death a week prior, begins receiving calls from listeners who also died last week — including, eventually, Marisol herself. The dead are trapped in a broadcast loop, an old folk song whose final verse was never recorded, and they need someone living to learn it without singing along. As every mirror in Sebastian's house begins lagging one second behind reality — then pulling them bodily into the reflected rooms — Sebastian must transcribe the verse from Marisol's humming while resisting the urge to answer her when she sings. In the end, Sebastian broadcasts the completed verse at 3:33 a.m., releasing the dead but learning that the price of survival is never hearing Marisol's voice again: the song takes the singer's memory of it, and with it, every recording, every voicemail, every echo of her.
about_author: Kestrel Joubert is the pen name of a former overnight radio engineer who spent six years alone in a station basement surrounded by dead air and older recordings than the station itself. They write horror about grief, signal, and the things that wait in the pause between songs.

chapters.title: Dead Air, Live Callers
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. A week after Marisol's funeral, Sebastian hosts 'The Night Line' as ritual self-punishment, until callers begin describing their own deaths in calm detail — all died last week, all humming the same half-remembered tune. Sebastian documents each call obsessively, telling themselves it's research. The emotional beat is denial sharpening into compulsion: documentation as prayer, grief disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV, fracturing into second person as the house turns against them. Every mirror reflects the room a beat late; then the reflections show Marisol, mouthing words. When a mirror pulls Sebastian fully inside, they find the dead listeners standing in the reflected kitchen, teaching fragments of the song's lost verse — but anyone who sings along joins the loop forever. Emotional beat: terror braided with longing, because the trap looks exactly like homecoming.

chapters.title: The Verse Without a Voice
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV under siege. Marisol appears in the studio glass during broadcast, singing the final verse line by line, and Sebastian realizes she's both trying to save them and being used as bait by whatever runs the loop. The mirrors begin pulling neighbors in; time collapses to a single night. Sebastian must memorize the verse by ear alone, writing it down without ever letting their own mouth shape it. Climactic beat: love weaponized, duty versus the desperate want to just sing with her.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV, resolved and hollowed. At 3:33 a.m., Sebastian reads the completed verse on air — spoken, never sung — and the loop breaks: the dead listeners dissolve mid-hum, Marisol mouths goodbye, and the mirrors snap back to honest time. But the song exacts its toll: every trace of Marisol's voice vanishes from the world and from Sebastian's memory of sound. Final beat: survival purchased at the price of the very thing worth surviving for; Sebastian signs off, and keeps broadcasting to no one.
